about: Every case is built around one way extraction goes wrong, and `forbid` is where that
trap is written down. Most of them are the same trap: a document states something
true about SOME course, and the model has no way to know it is not this one. A model
reading the ninth problem set of a term has never seen the other eight, so the course
header at the top of the page looks exactly like a discovery.
The text is written rather than scraped, deliberately. A corpus of the student's own
documents cannot be committed, and a corpus of one course's real files would tune the
prompts to that course's formatting. Add real documents locally with a `path` key on
a case; the harness reads it relative to this file.

ECE 301: Signals and Systems
Spring 2026 Course Syllabus

Instructor: Dr. Amara Osei
Email: aosei@example.edu
Office hours: Tuesdays and Thursdays, 2-4pm, Engineering Building room 3.14

Prerequisites
Students are expected to have completed a course in linear algebra and to be comfortable with complex arithmetic. Familiarity with MATLAB is assumed.

Course Description
This course covers continuous and discrete time signals, linear time-invariant systems, convolution, Fourier series, the Fourier transform, and the Laplace transform. The final third of the term treats sampling and the z-transform.

Grading
Problem sets are worth 30% of the final grade. The midterm exam is worth 25%. The final exam is worth 40%. Participation accounts for the remaining 5%. Late work loses 10% per day, and no work is accepted more than three days after the deadline.

Schedule
Midterm 1 will be held on 2026-03-04 in the main hall.
The final exam is scheduled for 2026-05-12.
Problem sets are due each Friday at 5pm.

Conventions
This course uses the engineering sign convention for the Fourier transform, with the forward transform carrying the factor e^{-jwt} and no leading 1/sqrt(2*pi). All work must show intermediate steps; an answer alone earns no credit.

cases.text:
ECE 205: Linear Systems - Fall 2019
Homework 3 Solutions
Prepared by the grading team under Professor J. Kowalski
Graders: return these to students only after the late deadline of 24 October 2019.

Problem 1. (20 marks)
Solution: The signal x(t) is periodic with period T = 2, so its Fourier series coefficients are a_k = (1/T) * integral over one period of x(t) e^{-jkw0t} dt. Evaluating gives a_0 = 1/2 and a_k = (1 - (-1)^k)/(j*2*pi*k) for k nonzero.

Problem 2. (20 marks)
Solution: By the time-shift property, shifting x(t) by t0 multiplies each coefficient by e^{-jkw0t0}. The magnitude spectrum is therefore unchanged and only the phase is affected.

Problem 3. (20 marks)
Solution: Parseval's relation gives the average power as the sum of |a_k|^2 over all k. Summing the series above yields an average power of 1/3.

cases.name: lecture-notes-state-a-convention-worth-keeping
cases.text:
Week 6 Lecture Notes: The z-Transform

Reading assignment for next lecture: chapter 10, sections 1 through 4.

Definition
The z-transform of a discrete-time signal x[n] is X(z) = sum over n of x[n] z^{-n}. In this course we always use the bilateral z-transform unless a problem says otherwise, and we always state the region of convergence alongside the transform. A z-transform written without its region of convergence is considered incomplete and will not receive full credit.

Region of convergence
The region of convergence is an annulus in the complex plane. For a right-sided signal it is the exterior of a circle through the outermost pole; for a left-sided signal it is the interior of a circle through the innermost pole.

Notation
We write the unit step as u[n] and the unit impulse as delta[n]. Note that some textbooks write the impulse as d[n]; we do not.

cases.text:
Signals and Systems, Second Edition
A. V. Oppenheim and A. S. Willsky
Prentice Hall, 1996

Chapter 7: Sampling

7.1 Representation of a Continuous-Time Signal by Its Samples

Under certain conditions a continuous-time signal is completely represented by its samples taken at uniform intervals. The sampling theorem states that a band-limited signal with no frequency components above w_M is uniquely determined by samples taken at a rate greater than 2*w_M, a rate known as the Nyquist rate.

7.2 Reconstruction

Reconstruction from samples is performed by an ideal lowpass filter, which in the time domain corresponds to interpolation with a sinc function. In practice a zero-order hold followed by a compensating filter is used.

7.3 Aliasing

When the sampling rate falls below the Nyquist rate, frequency components above half the sampling rate are folded down and become indistinguishable from lower-frequency components. This phenomenon is called aliasing.

Problems at the end of this chapter should be attempted after reading section 7.3.

MATH 118 - handout
R. Hendricks, room 204, Mondays
revised 2021

A matrix A is diagonalizable when there exists an invertible P such that P^{-1}AP is diagonal. This happens exactly when A has a full set of linearly independent eigenvectors.

The characteristic polynomial is det(A - lambda*I). Its roots are the eigenvalues. An eigenvalue whose algebraic multiplicity exceeds its geometric multiplicity is called defective, and a matrix with a defective eigenvalue is not diagonalizable.
